definitions.meaning: belonging to the Isle of Man, whose capital town is this
a man's first name, as in the actor Kirk

explanation.surface: A phrase about one man belonging to another.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital 'M' hides the Isle of Man, the island in the Irish Sea; the second word is just any man, here a first name.
explanation.definitionFit: Douglas is the capital of the Isle of Man and also a common male forename.

definitions.meaning: Charles Montagu ... wrote Travels in Arabia Deserta

explanation.surface: A tribute to a fearsome travel-writer.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means stout-hearted and formidable, and Charles Doughty wrote a classic of travel in Arabia.

clue.text: Here Dr. Johnson stood repentant in the rain

definitions.text: Here Dr. Johnson stood repentant in the rain

parts.words: Here Dr. Johnson stood repentant in the rain
parts.note: Samuel Johnson did penance bareheaded in the rain at a market town where his father had kept a bookstall

explanation.surface: A biographical fact about Samuel Johnson.
explanation.walkthrough: As an old man Johnson stood in the market place of this Staffordshire town to atone for refusing, as a boy, to help at his father's bookstall there.
explanation.definitionFit: The Staffordshire market town is where Johnson famously did penance in the rain.

clue.text: So flax was known to the Romans

definitions.text: So flax was known to the Romans

parts.words: So flax was known to the Romans
parts.note: the Latin word for flax, still its botanical genus name

explanation.surface: A fact about the Roman name for a plant.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin word for flax remains the genus name of the plant.

clue.text: Venetian-blind component, sets of three, not for the houseproud

parts.note: a Venetian blind is made of horizontal slats
a tern is a set of three, as in a winning lottery triple

explanation.surface: A list of household items that a fussy homemaker would avoid.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition describes the women rather than naming them: people who are anything but houseproud.
explanation.definitionFit: These are untidy, slovenly women, the opposite of house-proud homemakers.

definitions.meaning: like Eugénie, Napoleon III's empress, whose name this word echoes

explanation.surface: A compliment on someone's fine breeding and regal bearing.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means concerned with good breeding, and it also reads as 'like Eugénie', the French empress.

clue.text: Low fire at the end of the month

definitions.meaning: a glowing remnant of a dying fire

definitions.text: at the end of the month
definitions.meaning: the last letters of September, November and December

explanation.surface: The fire dies down as the month closes.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading is literal: the last four months' names all end in these five letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A glowing coal is what is left of a fire, and the letters close the names of the last months.

definitions.meaning: a large marine mammal, a big flippered swimmer
the seal of the realm, used to impress, or stamp, the nation's most important documents

explanation.surface: A big swimmer starring in a stunning documentary film.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a large marine mammal and also the chief seal of the realm, pressed onto state documents.

indicators.note: as here hints that the letters of the word before it are recast, the only signal of the rearrangement

explanation.surface: Victims slain the way the biblical Jael kills.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram is barely signalled: SLAIN, recast, gives the verb. In Judges, Jael kills Sisera by driving a tent peg through his temple.
explanation.definitionFit: Jael fastens Sisera's head to the ground with a tent peg, so she fixes him with a spike.

parts.note: the real surname of the writer whose pen name sounds like two

explanation.surface: One name shared by a pair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'two' is Twain: Mark Twain's real name was Samuel Langhorne Clemens.
explanation.definitionFit: Samuel Clemens wrote as Mark Twain, and twain is an old word for two.

clue.text: Rising to the north was seen the House Beautiful

parts.note: rising means going up
taken as written
N is the standard abbreviation for north

explanation.surface: A traveller climbing northwards catches sight of a splendid house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'was seen' is only a link. Upton House in Warwickshire is a celebrated country house, here given a name from Bunyan's 'House Beautiful'.
explanation.definitionFit: Upton House is a famous stately home, a beautiful house worth the name.

clue.text: Here I'd see Lamb, perhaps, and possibly Wordsworth

indicators.note: perhaps says the letters of the phrase before it may be arranged differently

explanation.surface: A Lake District visitor hopes to spot Charles Lamb and maybe Wordsworth too.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges I'D SEE LAMB. The tail 'and possibly Wordsworth' adds colour: Wordsworth lived at Rydal Mount nearby, so you might well meet him there.
explanation.definitionFit: The clue's 'here' points to a place, this town at the head of Windermere in the Lake District.

parts.note: not a tall person in a queue but a verse line of six metrical feet

explanation.surface: A very tall man standing in a queue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'six-footer' suggests height, but the feet are metrical ones, and 'lined up' means set out as one line of verse.
explanation.definitionFit: The classical epic metre has six feet to every line.

clue.text: It shows a nice arrangement of buds

definitions.text: It shows a nice arrangement of buds

parts.words: It shows a nice arrangement of buds
parts.note: nice in its old sense of discriminating: a fine judgment, and the tongue's buds that give the sense of flavour

explanation.surface: A flower display with pleasingly arranged buds.
explanation.walkthrough: The buds look floral; they are the ones on the tongue, and 'nice' means fastidious, as in a nice distinction.
explanation.definitionFit: Discernment in matters of style shows in a fine arrangement, and the tongue's buds are named after this sense.

clue.text: Novelist seen in many a Test

indicators.note: seen in says the name lies inside the following words, running across them

explanation.surface: A writer often spotted watching cricket Test matches.
explanation.walkthrough: Dornford Yates wrote popular thrillers between the wars; a Test is an international cricket match.
explanation.definitionFit: Dornford Yates was a best-selling English writer of fiction.

clue.text: Representative of northern landed interests in Parliament

definitions.text: Representative of northern landed interests in Parliament

parts.words: Representative of northern landed interests in Parliament
parts.note: in Cumbrian dialect, a small landowner; also a leading politician in Parliament

explanation.surface: An MP speaking for northern landowners.
explanation.walkthrough: In the Lake District the word meant a yeoman farming his own land; in Parliament it means a senior political figure.
explanation.definitionFit: A senior politician sits in Parliament, and in northern dialect the word meant a farmer owning his land.

parts.note: abstraction in its sense of taking away: things removed by force

explanation.surface: Powerful abstract ideas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'abstractions' looks like ideas; it means removals, and taking with force is what separates these crimes from theft.
explanation.definitionFit: These are thefts carried out with violence or the threat of it.

clue.text: Many people are taken by the power of his clutch

definitions.text: Many people are taken by the power of his clutch

parts.words: Many people are taken by the power of his clutch
parts.note: not a strong grip but a pedal: his passengers travel by the gearing he controls

explanation.surface: A strongman who carries off crowds in his grip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'clutch' suggests a grasp; it is the pedal, and 'taken' means carried as passengers.
explanation.definitionFit: He operates the clutch of a vehicle that carries many passengers.

clue.text: Source of ammunition for slingers attacking in columns

definitions.text: Source of ammunition for slingers attacking in columns

parts.words: Source of ammunition for slingers attacking in columns
parts.note: the slingers sling ink, and the columns are newspaper columns

explanation.surface: A supply of stones for soldiers marching in formation.
explanation.walkthrough: Slingers and columns suggest an ancient army; they are journalists 'slinging ink' at targets in newspaper columns.
explanation.definitionFit: Writers who attack opponents in print dip their pens in this container.

parts.note: the feet of 11 are metrical, and poets climb a mountain sacred to the Muses

explanation.surface: A mountain climbed on foot.
explanation.walkthrough: The feet are those of the verse line at 11, and the mountain is the Greek home of the Muses, where poets are said to climb.
explanation.definitionFit: This Greek mountain was sacred to Apollo and the Muses, so poetry is pictured as climbing it.

parts.note: a line from Shakespeare's Henry VI Part 1 about Joan of Arc, called there the Maid

explanation.surface: Astonishment that a young woman is so warlike.
explanation.walkthrough: In Henry VI Part 1, Charles says this of Joan of Arc, whom the play calls Joan la Pucelle, French for the Maid.
explanation.definitionFit: The French title for Joan of Arc means the maid, the girl who led armies.

parts.note: with 12's answer put in, a phrase meaning to be fond of something

explanation.surface: A cross-reference phrase saying someone has a fondness.
explanation.walkthrough: Put the answer to 12 into the gap and the phrase means to enjoy or be fond of something.
explanation.definitionFit: Having a relish for something is the same as being fond of it.

parts.note: the meaning of the Old English name of an island in the Thames estuary

explanation.surface: A title for an island of grazing flocks.
explanation.walkthrough: The Isle of Sheppey lies off the north Kent coast; its name comes from Old English for sheep island.
explanation.definitionFit: The Kent island's name derives from Old English words meaning isle of sheep.

parts.note: not a shop without a sign but a supply kept secret

explanation.surface: A shop with no sign outside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Store' looks like a shop; it is a stock, and 'not signposted' means hidden away.
explanation.definitionFit: A hidden hoard of supplies is kept where nobody can find it.

definitions.meaning: a thin snack eaten in a bite, the potato chip of British packets

explanation.surface: A hard, snappy mouthful.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain this is the word for a packet potato chip.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means firm and brittle, and it is also a thin fried potato snack.

clue.text: Song suggestive of a dog's stage part

indicators.note: suggestive of says the answer sounds like the phrase that follows

parts.note: a dog's part on stage would be to bark a role

explanation.surface: A song that hints at a dog's part in a play.
explanation.walkthrough: A dog playing a role would 'bark a role', which is how the Venetian gondolier's song sounds.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a Venetian gondolier's song, or music in its rocking rhythm.

definitions.meaning: holds back or lessens, as in holding your breath
Miss ..., the endlessly chattering spinster of Jane Austen's Emma

explanation.surface: Someone holds back the chatterbox.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means holds back, and Miss Bates is the talkative spinster in Austen's Emma.

clue.text: Hay in the extremes of the cold South

indicators.note: extremes of keeps only the outer ends of the word for the region, dropping its middle

parts.note: the frozen southern continent and region around the South Pole

explanation.surface: Hay stored at the frozen ends of the earth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'extremes of' keeps ANT and IC from ANTARCTIC, dropping ARCT. The definition comes from the phrase 'antic hay', a grotesque dance in Marlowe and the title of a Huxley novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Marlowe's phrase antic hay names a wild, grotesque dance, the adjective going with that dance.

parts.note: music tied to a particular character in an opera

explanation.surface: Music with a distinctive personality.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of character' sounds like praise, but it means belonging to a character: a recurring theme marking a person, as in Wagner.
explanation.definitionFit: Wagner's operas attach a recurring musical theme to each person or idea.

clue.text: Get to your feet, child, adders are active !

parts.note: a tot is a small child
get up means stand

explanation.surface: A parent tells a child to stand up because snakes are about.
explanation.walkthrough: The adders are not snakes but people adding numbers; the phrase means to add up.
explanation.definitionFit: To add up a column of figures is what people adding do.

parts.note: grows larger in every direction

explanation.surface: Prices or figures going up across the board.
explanation.definitionFit: To swell outwards in every direction is to grow in size.

definitions.meaning: Al Capone ran a racket, so his career was of the racket kind

explanation.surface: A gangster's career was a loud one.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means clattering and loud, and also reads as 'racket-like', the gangster's criminal trade.
